options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Average-Cost Decision Fallacy): Current ATC includes fixed rent that must be paid regardless; comparing price to ATC ignores that the extra loaves only cost $13.00 each to bake.

options_template.text: No, because producing 30 loaves will force the bakery to pay an extra $200 in daily fixed rent.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Variable-Fixed-Cost Fallacy): Short-run fixed rent does not increase when daily output expands from 20 to 30 loaves.

options_template.text: Yes, because producing 10 more loaves lowers Marginal Cost to zero.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Zero-MC Fallacy): Marginal Cost is $13.00 per loaf—not zero—yet the order is still worthwhile because $15.00 exceeds $13.00.

options_template.text: Yes, because the $15.00 price exceeds the $13.00 Marginal Cost, adding $20.00 to daily profit (or reducing losses by $20.00) while fixed rent remains unchanged.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Incremental decisions compare marginal benefit ($15/loaf) to marginal cost ($13/loaf); because fixed costs are unaffected, accepting the order improves the bottom line by ($15 - $13) * 10 = $20.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Resolving Rising MC with Falling ATC
questions.title: Diagnosing an Apparent Paradox: Rising MC Alongside Falling ATC
questions.prompt_template: In the bakery's daily cost schedule, Marginal Cost rises from $8.00 per loaf (between 10 and 20 loaves) to $13.00 per loaf (between 20 and 30 loaves), yet Average Total Cost falls from $19.00 to $17.00 over the exact same expansion. A student claims the accounting table must contain an arithmetic error. How do you resolve this apparent paradox?

hints.text: Compare the new Marginal Cost ($13.00) against the prior Average Total Cost ($19.00), not against the earlier Marginal Cost ($8.00).
Apply the cumulative GPA analogy from Section 6.2.

options_template.text: There is no error: even though MC is rising (from $8 to $13), MC ($13) is still below ATC ($19), so the extra loaves are cheaper than the existing average and continue pulling ATC downward.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Just as earning a 3.20 after a 2.80 raises your semester grade yet still pulls down a 3.60 cumulative GPA, a rising MC that remains below ATC still pulls ATC downward.

options_template.text: The table contains an error because ATC can only fall when MC is also falling.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Slope-Matching Fallacy): ATC falls whenever MC < ATC, regardless of whether MC itself is rising or falling.

options_template.text: There is no error because fixed costs must have fallen between 20 and 30 loaves.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Changing-FC Fallacy): Total fixed cost stays constant at $200; it is AFC falling (and MC < ATC) that brings ATC down from $19 to $17.

options_template.text: The table contains an error because MC must always exceed ATC once diminishing marginal product begins.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Immediate-Crossover Fallacy): Diminishing returns cause MC to start rising well before MC climbs high enough to cross above ATC.

questions.taxonomy: Tier 4: Critical Thinking / Empirical Policy Application
questions.topic: Short-Run vs. Long-Run Response to Permanent Demand Growth
questions.title: Adjusting Production Capacity After a Permanent Surge in Demand
questions.prompt_template: A regional bakery operating a small plant experiences a permanent doubling of customer demand. Initially, its per-loaf cost spikes as it pushes overtime shifts inside its existing small bakery; two years later, after building a larger regional facility, its per-loaf cost drops below its original pre-surge level. How do the short-run and long-run cost curves capture this two-stage adjustment?

hints.text: Distinguish moving along a fixed SRATC_small curve in the short run from transitioning to a new SRATC_medium curve along the LRATC envelope in the long run.
Check why per-loaf cost first rose (short-run crowding) and later fell below the original level (economies of scale).

options_template.text: In the short run the firm slid down its LRATC curve, and in the long run it suffered diminishing marginal product.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Reversed Horizon Dynamics): Moving along LRATC requires changing plant size (long run), while short-run overtime crowding triggers diminishing marginal product.

options_template.text: In the short run the firm moved up the rising portion of SRATC_small due to fixed-capital crowding; in the long run it built a larger plant along the downward-sloping economies-of-scale portion of LRATC.
options_template.feedback: Correct. Locked into its small plant initially, the firm moved rightward up SRATC_small (higher ATC); in the long run, scaling all inputs to a larger plant captured economies of scale and lowered per-unit cost along LRATC.

options_template.text: The initial cost spike proves the bakery experienced diseconomies of scale, and the later cost drop occurred because the bakery eliminated all variable costs.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Mislabeling & Zero-VC Fallacy): Short-run crowding is diminishing marginal product, not diseconomies of scale, and a larger bakery still pays variable costs for ingredients and labor.

options_template.text: Both stages occurred along the exact same SRATC_small curve as Average Fixed Cost rose and then fell.
options_template.feedback: Diagnostic fallacy (Single-Curve Fallacy): Building a larger regional facility changes fixed capital and shifts the firm onto a completely different SRATC curve, and AFC never rises with higher output.
